candidates.title: CASTLE: training natural language search before the first real query
candidates.summary: How we addressed the cold-start problem for Airbnb’s natural language search by jointly generating synthetic training data — queries and relevance labels — from de-identified booking and search signals. By : Wendy Ran Wei , Hao Li , Weiwei Guo , Xiaowei Liu , Xueyin Chen , Chun How Tan , Malay Haldar , Soumyadip Banerjee , Kedar Bellare , Huiji Gao , Sanjeev Katariya , and Stephanie Moyerman Introduction Natural language search lets guests express intent in their own words, such as “romantic cabin near skiing” or “pet-friendly beach house that sleeps eight,” rather than navigating filters and categories. We needed to introduce this kind of search for Airbnb, and to have it work well from the start. However, this required training the model before we had actual user queries to train the model on, and a reasonable set of relevance labels (inferred from the queries) to map queries to matching listings. Without prior traffic, both must be synthesized from scratch. This is the cold-start problem for natural-language search. Other organizations have faced similar challenges and have created methods to address them. However, prior approaches address the need for a body of queries and the need for relevance labels separately. Passage-based methods such as InPars [1] prompt a large language model (LLM) to generate queries conditioned on a single document, then rely on additional LLM judgments to assign relevance labels, introducing a second source of error. candidates.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
candidates.summary: As our merges per day grew more than tenfold, source control became our biggest development bottleneck. Here, we share how we migrated to an in-house version control system in five months.
